title: Denis Villeneuve explains Dune: Part Three's Chani changes
body_md:
Denis Villeneuve has identified Chani as the character at the center of one of his most significant departures from Frank Herbert's Dune novels. In an interview with TIME, as reported in the source article, the filmmaker explained how that decision began with Dune: Part Two and will continue to shape the relationship between Chani, played by Zendaya, and Paul Atreides, played by Timothee Chalamet, in Dune: Part Three.

**This article discusses the ending of Dune: Part Two but does not reveal the third film's ending.**

## A change that began in Part Two

Villeneuve described a challenge he faced while adapting Herbert's first novel: communicating the author's warning about messianic leadership without allowing Paul's rise to power to read simply as a triumphant heroic journey.

At the end of the first book, Paul wins a decisive conflict, becomes emperor, marries a princess and retains his relationship with Chani. Villeneuve felt that the structure could encourage readers to interpret the outcome as a celebration of the protagonist, even though the broader story challenges that interpretation.

The filmmaker therefore made Chani more openly skeptical of the idea that an outsider should become the Fremen people's savior. His adaptation also introduces a generational division in attitudes toward religious prophecies. Younger Fremen who question those beliefs advocate liberation through their own efforts rather than dependence on an appointed messiah.

Chani embodies that resistance, giving the audience a perspective from which to question Paul's choices without abandoning the emotional connection between them.

## Love for Paul and resistance to his regime

Villeneuve says that Chani's critical stance continues in the third movie. Her opposition is directed toward the regime Paul has established rather than a desire to harm him personally. This distinction places political and ethical disagreement alongside the characters' romantic history.

Although Dune: Part Three adapts Dune Messiah, the filmmaker's comments suggest that Chani's development will not simply reproduce every aspect of her literary counterpart's journey. Villeneuve also expressed a wish that he could have discussed these creative decisions with Herbert himself.

The approach could reinforce the series' examination of concentrated power and unquestioning loyalty to charismatic leaders. However, the interview does not establish whether Chani's ultimate fate will differ from the novel, and any claim about the film's final resolution would remain speculative.

Dune: Part Three is scheduled to reach theaters on December 18, 2026. Its release will reveal how Villeneuve brings this particular reinterpretation of Herbert's themes into the conclusion of his trilogy.
